title: How do you write a fitness UGC script without promising results?
description: How to write a fitness UGC script that films the routine, the effort and the product in use, with no body-change promises and an example script to adapt.
short_answer: A fitness UGC script sells the routine you can film, not a body you cannot promise. Show where the product fits in a real session, say what you noticed while using it, and keep every line about your own experience, so the viewer judges the product and not a result nobody can see yet.

sections.heading: Why do fitness UGC scripts drift into promises?

blocks.text: Results depend on the person, so a line about how someone's body will change is a promise you cannot film.

The pull toward promises starts with the opening line. A fitness [hook](/glossary/#hook) wants a big reason to keep watching, and the quickest big reason is a body that looks different. Resist it before you write a word. Read the [brief](/glossary/#brief) for the lines you must use and the claims you must avoid, and treat that list as fixed. Marking up the brief is covered step by step in [how to turn a brand brief into a script](/blog/brief-to-script/), and doing it first means nothing slips through once you start drafting.

Then write every line in the first person and about the past or the present: what you did, what you noticed, what you changed in your week. That keeps the script about your experience, which you can stand behind, instead of the viewer's future, which you can't.

sections.heading: What can a fitness script show instead of results?

blocks.text: It can show the routine, the effort, the setup and how the product feels in use, because all of those happen in front of the camera.

table_rows: The band going round your wrists and the first slow rep.
The viewer sees the product as a tool, not an outcome.
Get fit without leaving your living room.
The space you cleared, the mat going down, the kit on the floor.
It proves the routine fits a real room.
The only workout you will ever need.
Where this session sits in your week, said plainly.
It sounds like a person talking, not an advert.
You'll feel amazing after one session.
Your face at the end of a hard set, and one honest line about it.
Effort is believable when the viewer can see it.

blocks.text: The formats that suit this are process formats: a routine walkthrough, one session from start to finish, a setup video, or a [POV video](/glossary/#pov-video) of the moment you decide to train anyway. Each one is built from things you did, so none of them needs a claim to hold the viewer. [How to write a POV video script](/blog/pov-video-script/) covers that last one in detail.

sections.heading: What should you say instead of a result?

blocks.text: Say what you noticed, what you did and what you would tell a friend, because those are true for you and need no promise.

items: Swap outcome words for sensation words. Instead of a line about getting toned, say where you felt the work, such as in your shoulders by the last set.
Describe the product, not the person. Talk about the grip, the weight, the noise it makes, how it packs away and how quickly you can set it up.
Describe your routine honestly. Say how often you use it in plain words, such as twice a week before work, and say nothing about where that routine will take anyone else.
Keep comparisons to your own past. You can say you used to skip sessions because the gym felt far away, as long as it is true for you.
Hand the claim back to the brand. If it wants a benefit mentioned, ask for the exact approved wording in writing and say only that.

blocks.text: If a line still sounds like a promise, test it against the camera: could you film proof of it in this video? If not, cut it or turn it into something you noticed. The same test sits behind [hook and payoff](/blog/hook-payoff/), because a hook can only promise what the rest of the video goes on to show. It also runs through [what goes in a UGC script for a skincare brand](/blog/ugc-script-for-skincare/), where results are just as personal and just as slow to film.

sections.heading: What does an honest fitness UGC script look like?

blocks.text: An honest fitness script follows one real session, lets the product appear where it actually fits, and closes by asking for one thing.

blocks.script_caption: Example script — written for this answer, for a set of fabric resistance bands

script_beats.say: My workouts kept losing to the drive to the gym.
script_beats.do: You stand by the front door with car keys in hand, then hang them back up.

script_beats.say: So this week I trained in the gap between the sofa and the coffee table.
script_beats.do: Wide shot as you push the table back and roll a mat out across the floor.

script_beats.say: These are fabric bands. They sit flat, so they don't roll up my legs halfway through a set.
script_beats.do: Close-up of the band sliding over your knees, then your hand smoothing it flat.

script_beats.say: Squats first. Slow on the way down, because that's where I feel it.
script_beats.do: Side-on shot of three slow squats, with your breathing left in the audio.

script_beats.say: The part I didn't expect was the quiet. No clanking, nothing for the flat downstairs to hear.
script_beats.do: Hold on the band and the floor as you finish a set in near silence.

script_beats.say: I've done this before work for a few weeks now. The bands I use are linked.
script_beats.do: You coil the bands into a small pouch and drop it into a drawer.

blocks.text: Notice what it never says. Nothing about how the creator's legs look, nothing about what the viewer will gain, and no line the camera can't back up. Lay your draft out as a [two-column script](/glossary/#two-column-script) like this one, so the brand can check every spoken line against what is on screen before you film.

sections.heading: What if the brand asks you to promise results?

blocks.text: Ask the brand for its approved claim wording in writing and use only that, because a claim is the brand's to make and stand behind, not yours.

If the request arrives as a note on a draft, reply with the line you can say and your reason for it. A short message keeps it calm: “I can only speak for my own sessions, so I'd rather not say how this will change anyone's body. I can describe what I noticed while using [PRODUCT], or use the wording your team has approved if you send it over.” That gives the brand two ways forward instead of a refusal.

If the change would still break the video, read [what to do when brand feedback would break the video](/blog/ugc-feedback-that-breaks-the-video/) for a way to explain the problem and offer a fix without losing the job.

hooks: My workouts kept losing to the drive to the gym.
